narrative:
The model determined that you have a 56% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Your rejection was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. By far the most influential was your third-year class ranking. Placing in the bottom decile of your class sent a strong signal that you were likely to struggle with the bar exam, pushing the prediction heavily toward failure. Your first-year ranking also mattered, though less so; being in the fourth decile rather than the sixth-decile average of accepted students added a modest additional concern. Finally, your undergraduate GPA of 2.40, well below the 3.23 average of admitted students, further increased the predicted risk of failure.

These academic performance indicators outweighed other details in your profile, such as your upper-middle family income or your plan to attend part-time. Even your LSAT score of 30, which sits noticeably below the 37 average of successful applicants, played a smaller role than your class rankings and college grades.

To improve your chances, you should focus on strengthening your academic foundation. Consider retaking key courses, enrolling in a structured bar-preparation program, or gaining additional legal experience that demonstrates your ability to handle rigorous material. With clearer evidence of improvement, future applications may be viewed more favorably. (218 words)
